questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why standards can be inefficient
questions.stem: Ticket 203 asks why a technology mandate is often costlier than a tax. Why?

options.text: It raises government spending
options.misconception: spending is not the efficiency issue

options.text: It forces all firms to use the same method regardless of cost
It eliminates all emissions
options.misconception: mandates rarely eliminate emissions

options.text: It lowers prices for consumers
options.misconception: mandates typically raise costs

questions.explanation: A mandate ignores cost differences across firms, forcing expensive methods. Spending and prices are secondary.
questions.hint: Same method for all ignores cost differences.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the efficient outcome of bargaining
questions.stem: cost of abatement is 200 and benefit is 350. Does efficient bargaining occur?

options.text: No, because rights are unclear
options.misconception: rights are stated as clear

options.text: No, because cost exceeds benefit
options.misconception: names "No, because cost exceeds benefit" where the rule requires "Yes, because benefit exceeds cost"

options.text: Yes, because benefit exceeds cost
Yes, but only with a tax
options.misconception: bargaining does not need a tax

questions.explanation: When benefit exceeds cost, gains from trade exist and bargaining is efficient. No tax is needed with clear rights.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute number of negotiators impact
questions.stem: 6 teams each must agree. If each additional team adds 10 units of coordination cost, total extra cost for all six?
questions.explanation: Six teams times 10 units of coordination cost equals 60. Bargaining reaches an efficient agreement only when the gains from trade exceed the costs of negotiating and enforcing it. Ignoring transaction costs is the common error.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why government provides public goods
questions.stem: Ticket 218 asks why a shared security scanner is publicly funded. Explain.

answer.exemplar: Because the scanner is non-excludable and non-rival, private firms cannot charge users, so government provision funded by taxes avoids free riding.

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this public goods item is: Free riding prevents private provision. That is why "Because the scanner is non-excludable and non-rival, private firms cannot charge users, so government provision funded by taxes avoids free riding" is the answer.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute subsidy cost to government
questions.stem: subsidy is 3 per unit and 100 units are produced. Government cost?
questions.explanation: Applying the subsidy for a positive externality rule — Multiply subsidy by quantity — yields "300". Reversing the reasoning would recover the given quantities.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify policy to eliminate deadweight loss
questions.stem: Ticket 228 asks which policy removes deadweight loss from a positive externality. Which?

options.text: No policy, since markets are efficient
options.misconception: names "No policy, since markets are efficient" where the rule requires "A per-unit subsidy equal to marginal external benefit"

options.text: A tax on the good
options.misconception: taxes worsen underproduction

options.text: A quota below current output
options.misconception: quotas reduce output further

options.text: A per-unit subsidy equal to marginal external benefit

questions.explanation: A subsidy equal to external benefit aligns private and social incentives, eliminating deadweight loss.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain peak-load pricing efficiency
questions.stem: Ticket 233 asks why peak-load pricing improves efficiency on a shared cluster. Explain.

answer.exemplar: Peak-load pricing rations scarce capacity to high-value users during congestion, reducing overuse and aligning private cost with social cost.

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this congestion pricing item is: Price rations scarce capacity. That is why "Peak-load pricing rations scarce capacity to high-value users during congestion, reducing overuse and aligning private cost with social cost" is the answer.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute cost savings from trade
questions.stem: without trade cost is 100, with trade cost is 70. What are the savings?
questions.explanation: Savings equal the difference, 100 minus 70, which is 30. Cap and trade fixes total emissions and lets permits be traded, so the market finds the least-cost allocation of abatement. Assuming a fixed cap raises costs in every firm is the common mistake.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compare total costs of two policies
questions.stem: Policy X costs 120, Policy Y costs 80 for the same emission reduction. Which is more efficient?

options.text: Policy X, because higher cost signals quality
options.misconception: higher cost is not better

options.text: Policy Y, because it achieves the same reduction at lower cost
They are equally efficient
options.misconception: same reduction does not mean same cost

options.text: Neither, because costs must be zero
options.misconception: abatement always has cost

questions.explanation: The cost of a command-and-control order principle here is: Lower cost for same reduction wins. On that basis "Policy Y, because it achieves the same reduction at lower cost" is correct, while "Policy X, because higher cost signals quality" higher cost is not better.
questions.hint: Lower cost for same reduction wins.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain Coase irrelevance of initial allocation
questions.stem: Ticket 248 asks whether the initial rights assignment affects the final efficient outcome under Coase. Does it?

options.text: Yes, efficiency requires rights to the victim
options.misconception: same irrelevance error

options.text: Yes, efficiency requires rights to the polluter
options.misconception: efficiency is independent of initial rights

options.text: No, the final allocation is efficient either way; only distribution changes
Only if transaction costs are high
options.misconception: high costs break Coase entirely

questions.explanation: With low transaction costs, bargaining reaches efficiency regardless of initial rights; only who pays changes.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify when to use regulation instead of bargaining
questions.stem: Ticket 253 asks when regulation beats private bargaining. Which condition?

options.text: When abatement cost is zero
options.misconception: zero cost removes the need for policy

options.text: When property rights are perfectly clear
options.misconception: clear rights favor bargaining

options.text: When only two parties are involved
options.misconception: few parties favor bargaining

options.text: When transaction costs are high and many parties are involved

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this transaction costs and bargaining item is: Many parties raise negotiation costs. That is why "When transaction costs are high and many parties are involved" is right. The option "When abatement cost is zero" (zero cost removes the need for policy) does not satisfy the rule.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute optimal public good quantity condition
questions.stem: sum of marginal benefits is 50 and marginal cost is 30. Provide how many more units?
questions.explanation: Applying the public goods rule — Provide if summed benefit exceeds cost — yields "1". Reversing the reasoning would recover the given quantities.
questions.hint: Provide if summed benefit exceeds cost.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain subsidy incidence
questions.stem: Ticket 263 asks who benefits from a subsidy on a positive externality. Explain.

answer.exemplar: Both producers and consumers benefit: producers receive a higher effective price and consumers pay a lower price, while output rises toward efficiency.

questions.explanation: The subsidy for a positive externality principle here is: Both sides gain via prices. On that basis "Both producers and consumers benefit: producers receive a higher effective price and consumers pay a lower price, while output rises toward efficiency" is correct.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute deadweight loss with given triangle
questions.stem: deadweight loss triangle base 8, height 3. What is the area?
questions.explanation: For a deadweight loss from external benefits question like this, the governing rule is: Use half base times height. Applying it gives "12" as the answer.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify who bears congestion cost
questions.stem: Ticket 273 asks who ultimately bears congestion cost without pricing. Which is correct?

options.text: Only the government
options.misconception: government does not bear private delay

options.text: All users through longer waits and delays
No one, because congestion is free
options.misconception: congestion imposes real time costs

options.text: Only new entrants
options.misconception: existing users also suffer delays

questions.explanation: Without pricing, congestion costs fall on all users as delays. Government and entrants are not the sole bearers.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain permit price as marginal abatement cost
questions.stem: Ticket 278 asks what the permit price represents in equilibrium. Explain.

answer.exemplar: In equilibrium the permit price equals the marginal abatement cost, so firms abate until their marginal cost matches the price.

questions.explanation: The cap and trade principle here is: Price equals marginal abatement cost. On that basis "In equilibrium the permit price equals the marginal abatement cost, so firms abate until their marginal cost matches the price" is correct.
